newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi Arabia to step up oil exports to China.
newsitem.headline: Saudi Arabia to step up oil exports to China.

text.p: Oil powerhouse Saudi Arabia will supply increasingly import-dependent China with more crude from the second half of this year, Saudi sources and Chinese officials in Saudi Arabia said on Tuesday.
"An understanding has been reached that Saudi Arabia will supply China with whatever they need starting in the second half of this year," a Saudi source told Reuters.
The pact was sealed in talks this week in Riyadh and Dhahran between officials from state-oil firm Saudi Aramco and Chinese state refiner Sinopec, Chinese and Saudi sources said.
Aramco is already a major supplier to China, supplying it with around 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) though the deal has not specified actual future sales volumes.
China's rapid-fire industrialisation is expected to double the country's crude imports to 50 million tonnes (one million barrels per day) by the year 2000.
Its own output of heavy, low sulphur crude has stagnated, prompting a long-term policy to add to and revamp existing refineries to run off similar crudes from the Middle East.
Supply deals with OPEC-member Iran and multi-billion dollar oilfield development contracts in Iraq and Kazakhstan have been struck by the Chinese government in May and June.

Iran's vice petroleum minister for trade, Ghanimi Fard, on Tuesday said that Tehran would increase its oil supply to Beijing from a current 70,000 barrels per day (bpd) to 100,000 bpd in 1998 and then 200,000 bpd by the year 2000.
Saudi joint-venture investment in Chinese refineries was also discussed at the meetings but there was no breakthrough in talks which have been ongoing since the start of the decade.
"Discussions continued but there is no final agreement reached yet," the Saudi source said.

Both sides are negotiating to build a new 200,000 bpd refinery at Qingdao in the eastern Chinese province of Shandong and at Koingto and also an expansion of the existing Maoming refinery, the largest plant in southern China.

Aramco is seeking to boost its presence in the Chinese market -- which accounts for around five percent of global oil demand and has the potential to edge closer to the U.S. and Japan as the world's largest oil consumers -- to tie up an increasing volume of its crude exports.
Through a stake in a South Korean firm, Aramco aleady has a controlling interest in the north-eastern Thalin refinery.

The state firm has also built up downstream stakes in United States, Philippines, South Korea and Greece and is aiming to secure retail outlets also in Portugal and India as well as China for its six million bpd-plus of crude exports.
Hurdles facing the proposed downstream deal at Qingdao include Aramco's demands that it be allowed full access to China's domestic market and financing arrangements.

Beijing has ruled that joint venture refineries involving foreigners must export at least 70 percent of their output to earn valuable foreign currency despite the potential massive home market of 1.2 billion people.

Under the proposed Qingdao joint venture Aramco would take a 45 percent stake in the new refinery, Chinese state-owned trader Sinochem 40 percent and South Korea's Ssangyong Oil Refining Co Ltd 15 percent.

A Chinese embassy official in Riyadh said that the Chinese delegation, led by Sinopec president Sheng Huaren was returning hone on Tuesday and that Saudi and Chinese officials hoped to sign a memorandum on increased energy cooperation.
Sinopec operates 38 refineries in China, representing 80 percent of the country's 4.3 million bpd refining capacity.
Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil producer and exporter with an OPEC supply quota of eight million bpd.
